title: The normalized free simplex has a natural chain coalgebra diagonal
statement:
Fix a commutative ring $\Lambda$ and the universes of [def-weil-size-convention]. Use simplices and monotone maps as in [def-weil-pbc-simplicial-set], chain complexes as in [def-weil-pbc-module-chain-complex-homology], and module tensors as in [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. For $n\geq0$, let $P(n)_r$ be the free $\Lambda$-module on the strictly increasing strings $0\leq i_0<\cdots<i_r\leq n$ for $r\geq0$, zero otherwise. Its differential is $\partial[i_0,\ldots,i_r]=\sum_{j=0}^{r}(-1)^j[i_0,\ldots,\widehat i_j,\ldots,i_r]$ for $r>0$, zero for $r=0$. For a monotone $\alpha:[m]\to[n]$, $P(\alpha)$ sends a basis string to its image string if the images are distinct and to zero otherwise. Let $F(n)$ be the simplicial module whose degree $r$ term is the free module on the monotone maps $[r]\to[n]$, with operators given by precomposition [def-weil-pbc-simplicial-object]. With $N$ as in [lem-cbc-dold-kan-normalization-equivalence], the map $q_n:N(F(n))\to P(n)$ which discards all noninjective basis strings is a natural isomorphism of chain complexes.

The maps
$$D_n[i_0,\ldots,i_r]=\sum_{a=0}^{r}[i_0,\ldots,i_a]\otimes[i_a,\ldots,i_r],\qquad \epsilon_n[i]=1,$$
with $\epsilon_n$ zero in positive degrees, are chain maps $D_n:P(n)\to P(n)\otimes_\Lambda P(n)$ and $\epsilon_n:P(n)\to\Lambda[0]$. Here $(C\otimes C')_r=\bigoplus_{a+b=r}C_a\otimes C'_b$ and $\partial(c\otimes c')=\partial c\otimes c'+(-1)^a c\otimes\partial c'$ for $c\in C_a$. They satisfy $(D_n\otimes\mathrm{id})D_n=(\mathrm{id}\otimes D_n)D_n$ and $(\epsilon_n\otimes\mathrm{id})D_n=\mathrm{id}=(\mathrm{id}\otimes\epsilon_n)D_n$, under the canonical tensor identifications. Every $P(\alpha)$ commutes with $D$ and $\epsilon$.

source.place: Higher Algebra (2017), Remark 1.2.3.16 (kernel and quotient normalization), Construction 1.2.3.22, Remarks 1.2.3.24–25, Example 1.2.3.26 (Alexander–Whitney, naturality and associativity), specialized to free simplices and their diagonal, printed pp.58–64. Read online 2026-10-17; archive WANTED. Stacks Tag 017V, simplicial.tex lemma-splitting-abelian-category, supplies the normalized/degenerate splitting, not the Alexander–Whitney theorem.

proof.text: Write $U(n)_r=F(n)_r$ and equip it with the alternating deletion differential, zero in degree zero. Each term of $\partial^2$ deleting positions $j<k$ occurs twice, with signs $(-1)^{j+k-1}$ and $(-1)^{j+k}$, so $\partial^2=0$ (degrees zero and one are immediate). Let $B(n)_r$ be the span of the weakly increasing strings with a repeated entry. If positions $k,k+1$ agree, every deletion except those two still has a repetition; deleting $k$ and $k+1$ gives the same string with opposite signs. Hence $\partial B(n)_r\subseteq B(n)_{r-1}$. The quotient $U(n)_r/B(n)_r$ is freely generated by the strictly increasing strings: the maps retaining, respectively including, these generators are inverse modulo $B(n)_r$. Its induced differential is exactly that of $P(n)$ in the statement. Denote the quotient map by $Q_n:U(n)\to P(n)$.

source.place: Remark 1.2.3.16; explicit free-string quotient and signed deletion calculation. Stacks Tag 017V supplies context only, not an invoked splitting theorem.

proof.text: Postcomposing strings by $\alpha:[m]\to[n]$ gives a map $U(m)\to U(n)$ commuting with deletion, since $\alpha$ applied after deletion gives exactly the same string as deletion after $\alpha$. It preserves $B$, because equal entries remain equal. Its induced quotient map is precisely $P(\alpha)$, including zero on every collapsed string. The identity and composition laws follow by postcomposing strings before passing to the quotient. Thus every $P(\alpha)$ is a chain map and $Q$ is natural. In the same way $F(n)$ is simplicial: precomposing two monotone maps equals precomposing their composite.

source.place: Remark 1.2.3.16; functoriality of the explicit quotient.

proof.text: In degree $r$ the map $d_j$ deletes position $j$ and $s_k$ repeats position $k$. The identities needed below follow on each string: $d_js_{j-1}=1$; for $i>j$, $d_i s_{j-1}=s_{j-1}d_{i-1}$ and $d_{i-1}d_j=d_jd_i$; for $j>k+1$, $d_js_k=s_kd_{j-1}$ and $s_{j-1}s_k=s_ks_{j-2}$. For example the last identity inserts duplicates in positions $k$ and $j-1$ in either order, shifting the later insertion by one. These equalities extend linearly because the strings generate the free modules. No simplicial-identity theorem beyond these direct descriptions is being assumed.

source.place: Remark 1.2.3.16; positive-face version of the relations used in the proof of Stacks Tag 017V (simplicial.tex, lemma-splitting-abelian-category and its preceding proof).

proof.text: For fixed $r>0$ put $T_j=1-s_{j-1}d_j$ on $U(n)_r$, $1\leq j\leq r$, and $p_r=T_1T_2\cdots T_r$, so $T_r$ acts first; put $p_0=1$. Starting with $u=x$, apply $u\leftarrow T_ju$ for $j=r,r-1,\ldots,1$. The descending induction invariant before this operation is $d_i u=0$ for every $i>j$, vacuous initially. Now $d_jT_ju=0$, and for $i>j$ Step 3 gives $d_iT_ju=d_i u-s_{j-1}d_{i-1}d_j u=d_i u-s_{j-1}d_jd_i u=0$. Therefore $p_rx\in\bigcap_{j=1}^r\ker d_j=N(F(n))_r$. Every correction is in $B(n)_r$, so $Q_np_r=Q_n$. If $x\in N(F(n))_r$, each $T_j$ fixes $x$, so $p_rx=x$.

source.place: Remark 1.2.3.16; explicit descending projection for the positive-face convention. This proves rather than invokes the needed part of the normalized/degenerate splitting.

proof.text: Every repeated string is $s_k y$ for a shorter weakly increasing string, hence the $s_k y$ span $B(n)_r$. For $j>k+1$, Step 3 gives $T_j s_k=s_k T'_{j-1}$, where $T'_{j-1}=1-s_{j-2}d_{j-1}$ acts in degree $r-1$. Move $s_k$ to the left successively through the operations $T_r,T_{r-1},\ldots,T_{k+2}$; the resulting element is still of the form $s_k z$. The next operation kills it, since $T_{k+1}s_k=(1-s_kd_{k+1})s_k=0$. All remaining operations preserve zero. Thus $p_r B(n)_r=0$, also trivially for $r=0$ where $B(n)_0=0$.

source.place: Remark 1.2.3.16; the degeneracy-annihilation calculation for the explicit projection.

proof.text: Define $q_n$ by restricting $Q_n$ to the submodule $N(F(n))$. It is surjective in every degree: lift an increasing basis string to $U(n)_r$ and apply $p_r$; Step 4 says its image under $Q_n$ is the original basis string. It is injective: if $x\in N(F(n))_r$ has $Q_nx=0$, then $x\in B(n)_r$ by Step 1, so $x=p_rx=0$ by Steps 4–5. On $N(F(n))_r$, the alternating differential of $U(n)$ is $d_0$, since every other face vanishes; this is exactly the differential defining $N$. Hence $q_n$ commutes with differentials. Its degreewise inverse also commutes with differentials by multiplying this equation by the two inverses. Postcomposition by $\alpha$ commutes with every face, so preserves $N$; the naturality of $Q$ from Step 2 restricts to naturality of $q$. The phrase 'discards all noninjective basis strings' therefore means the restriction of this quotient map, not the assertion that the increasing strings themselves lie in the kernel normalization.

source.place: Remark 1.2.3.16; explicit kernel/quotient comparison for free simplices.

proof.text: The displayed total tensor has a well-defined differential: the module tensor universal property extends each bilinear formula, and on $c\otimes c'$ of bidegree $(a,b)$ its square is $\partial^2c\otimes c'+((-1)^{a-1}+(-1)^a)\partial c\otimes\partial c'+c\otimes\partial^2c'=0$; terms with a degree-zero differential are simply absent. The formulas for $D_n$ and $\epsilon_n$ extend uniquely linearly from the free generators. Each summand of $D_n$ has bidegree $(a,r-a)$, so has total degree $r$. Tensor associativity and the unit identifications used in the statement can be defined here by $(c\otimes c')\otimes c''\mapsto c\otimes(c'\otimes c'')$, $\lambda\otimes c\mapsto\lambda c$, and $c\otimes\lambda\mapsto\lambda c$. The inverse maps send $c\otimes(c'\otimes c'')$ to $(c\otimes c')\otimes c''$, and send $c$ to $1\otimes c$ and $c\otimes1$, respectively. Composing in either order fixes every pure tensor, by bilinearity, so these are isomorphisms. The total differential commutes with the associator: on a triple pure tensor the three signs are $1,(-1)^a,(-1)^{a+b}$ in both parenthesizations. For the units, the scalar factor lies in degree zero with zero differential, so both unit maps send the tensor differential to $\lambda\partial c=\partial(\lambda c)$; their inverses satisfy the same equation with $\lambda=1$. For degree-preserving chain maps $f,g$, define $(f\otimes g)(c\otimes c')=f(c)\otimes g(c')$. Its differential is $f(\partial c)\otimes g(c')+(-1)^a f(c)\otimes g(\partial c')$ on either side of the chain-map equation; thus the tensor maps in the identities below are chain maps whenever their factors are.

source.place: Remark 1.2.3.21 and Example 1.2.3.26; tensor differentials and constraints verified directly on pure tensors.

proof.text:
Fix $r>0$ and abbreviate $[i_u,\ldots,i_v]$ by $[u:v]$. Expanding $\partial D_n[0:r]$ gives precisely
$$\sum_{a=1}^r\sum_{j=0}^a(-1)^j[0:\widehat j:a]\otimes[a:r]+\sum_{a=0}^{r-1}\sum_{j=a}^r(-1)^j[0:a]\otimes[a:\widehat j:r].$$
The first sum comes from differentiating the front factor; the second has sign $(-1)^a(-1)^{j-a}=(-1)^j$. For $1\leq a\leq r$, its first-sum term with $j=a$ cancels the second-sum term indexed by $(a-1,j=a-1)$, since their tensors are both $[0:a-1]\otimes[a:r]$ and their signs are opposite. Every remaining first-sum term has $j<a$ and is the term of $D_n\partial[0:r]$ obtained by deleting $j$ and splitting at the surviving vertex $a$. Every remaining second-sum term has $j>a$ and is the corresponding term obtained by deleting $j$ and splitting at $a$. These alternatives enumerate every splitting after one deletion exactly once, with sign $(-1)^j$. Thus $\partial D_n=D_n\partial$. For $r=0$, both differentials are zero. Here brackets with a hat mean the indicated list with that entry deleted.

source.place: Construction 1.2.3.22; full finite-sum chain-map verification of its front/back formula, specialized to the diagonal of a free simplex.

proof.text: To check $\epsilon_n$ is a chain map it suffices to check basis strings. For $r=1$, $\epsilon_n\partial[i_0,i_1]=\epsilon_n([i_1]-[i_0])=1-1=0$. For $r>1$, the boundary has positive degree and is killed by $\epsilon_n$; for $r=0$ both differentials vanish. The target $\Lambda[0]$ has zero differential in every degree, giving the required chain-map equation in all cases.

On $[i_0,\ldots,i_r]$, the two iterated diagonals are both
$$\sum_{0\leq a\leq b\leq r}[i_0,\ldots,i_a]\otimes[i_a,\ldots,i_b]\otimes[i_b,\ldots,i_r].$$
Indeed, the left iteration first chooses the cut $b$ and then the cut $a\leq b$ in its front factor; the right iteration first chooses $a$ and then $b\geq a$ in its back factor. Tensor associativity is the pure-tensor identification of Step 7, and there are no signs because $D_n$ has degree zero. In $(\epsilon_n\otimes1)D_n$ only the cut $a=0$ survives, and its value under the unit identification is the original string. In $(1\otimes\epsilon_n)D_n$ only $a=r$ survives, with the same value. This proves coassociativity and both counit identities on generators and hence everywhere.

source.place: Remarks 1.2.3.24–25 and Example 1.2.3.26; explicit double-cut and end-cut calculations.

proof.text: Finally let $\alpha:[m]\to[n]$ be monotone and $\sigma=[i_0,\ldots,i_r]$ strictly increasing. If the values $\alpha(i_j)$ are distinct, applying $P(\alpha)\otimes P(\alpha)$ to each front/back summand gives exactly the corresponding summand of $D_nP(\alpha)\sigma$. Otherwise monotonicity gives an adjacent equality $\alpha(i_k)=\alpha(i_{k+1})$. At any cut $a\leq k$ the back factor contains this adjacent pair, and at any cut $a\geq k+1$ the front factor contains it. Thus every summand is killed on the tensor side; the other side is zero because $P(\alpha)\sigma=0$. This proves diagonal naturality even for noninjective $\alpha$. Augmentation naturality holds because all vertices still map to vertices with augmentation $1$, while positive-degree generators are either sent to positive-degree generators or zero, both with augmentation zero.

source.place: Remark 1.2.3.24; explicit check including every collapsed string, with no injectivity assumption on the monotone map.
